### 4.1 Turning Effects & Equilibrium - Easy

::: {.question-card}
#### Easy Q1 · Centre of gravity

What is the centre of gravity of an object?

A. the geometrical centre of the object

B. the point about which the total torque is zero

C. the point at which the weight of the object may be considered to act

D. the point through which gravity acts

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: C.** The centre of gravity is the point at which the whole weight of the object may be considered to act. Option A is true only for regular, uniform shapes. Option B describes the centre of rotational equilibrium.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Easy Q6 · Resultant moment about a pivot

A uniform metre rule of weight 4.0 N is pivoted at the 60 cm mark. A 6.0 N weight is suspended from one end, causing the rule to rotate about the pivot.

At the instant when the rule is horizontal, what is the resultant turning moment about the pivot?

|  | Resultant moment | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| A | 2.0 N m | clockwise |
| B | 2.0 N m | anticlockwise |
| C | 2.8 N m | clockwise |
| D | 2.8 N m | anticlockwise |

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: A.** The rule is uniform, so its weight acts at the 50 cm mark, 0.10 m from the pivot; this gives an anticlockwise moment of $4.0\times0.10=0.40\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. The 6.0 N weight at the end is 0.40 m from the pivot, giving a clockwise moment of $6.0\times0.40=2.4\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. The resultant moment is $2.0\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ clockwise.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Easy Q8 · Minimum force on a door

The diagram shows a plan view of a door which requires a moment of 14 N m to open it. The hinge is at one end and the door width is 0.7 m.

What is the minimum force that must be applied at the door's midpoint to ensure it opens?

A. 4.9 N

B. 9.8 N

C. 20 N

D. 40 N

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: D.** The midpoint is at $0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ from the hinge. The minimum force is $F=\text{moment}/d=14/0.35=40\ \mathrm{N}$.
</details>
:::

### 4.1 Turning Effects & Equilibrium - Medium

::: {.question-card}
#### Medium Q1 · Mass of a metre rule

A uniform metre rule is hung from the ceiling as shown. The string supports the rule at the 35 cm mark. The rule balances when a 75 g mass is hung from one end of the ruler.

What is the mass of the metre rule?

A. 38 g

B. 51 g

C. 141 g

D. 159 g

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: C.** The rule is uniform, so its weight acts at the 50 cm mark. Taking moments about the support, the weight of the rule balances the 75 g mass on the opposite side of the support. The official answer key gives 141 g, obtained with the pivot and load positions printed on the original question diagram.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Medium Q4 · Equilibrium while moving

An object, made from two equal masses joined by a light rod, falls with uniform speed through air. The rod remains horizontal.

Which statement about this system is correct?

A. It is not in equilibrium because it is falling steadily.

B. It is not in equilibrium because it is in motion.

C. It is not in equilibrium because there is a resultant torque.

D. It is in equilibrium because there is no resultant force and no resultant torque.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: D.** At uniform speed the acceleration is zero, so the resultant force is zero. The two equal masses produce equal and opposite moments, so the resultant torque is zero. A body moving at constant velocity can be in equilibrium.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Medium Q7 · Spindle, lever and disc

A spindle is attached at one end to the centre of a lever of length 1.60 m and at its other end to the centre of a disc of radius 0.25 m. A string is wrapped round the disc, passes over a pulley and is attached to an 800 N weight.

What is the minimum force $F$, applied to each end of the lever, that could lift the weight?

A. 62.5 N

B. 125 N

C. 250 N

D. 750 N

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: B.** The anticlockwise moment produced by the weight is $800\times0.25=200\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. The couple from the two equal lever forces gives a clockwise moment of $F\times1.60$. Equating: $F=200/1.60=125\ \mathrm{N}$.
</details>
:::

### 4.1 Turning Effects & Equilibrium - Hard

::: {.question-card}
#### Hard Q1 · Hanging a picture from a nail

The diagrams show two ways of hanging the same picture. In both cases, a string is attached to the same points on the picture and looped symmetrically over a nail. In diagram 1, the string loop is shorter than in diagram 2.

Which information about the magnitude of the forces is correct?

A. $R_1=R_2$, $T_1<T_2$

B. $R_1=R_2$, $T_1>T_2$

C. $R_1>R_2$, $T_1<T_2$

D. $R_1<R_2$, $T_1=T_2$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: B.** The picture has the same weight in both cases, so the resultant force on the nail is the same: $R_1=R_2$. With the shorter loop, the string makes a smaller angle to the vertical, so the tension in each string must be larger to support the same weight: $T_1>T_2$.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Hard Q3 · Bowstring resultant force

An archer draws his bowstring back to position X: tension $T=110\ \mathrm{N}$ in each half of the string, with the two halves at $120^\circ$ to each other. He then draws the bowstring back further to position Y: tension $T=150\ \mathrm{N}$ in each half, with the two halves at $90^\circ$ to each other.

The archer finds the resultant force on the arrow is greater when the arrow is released from position Y.

What is the increase in force?

A. 51 N

B. 55 N

C. 102 N

D. 110 N

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: C.** At X the resultant force is $2T\cos(120^\circ/2)=2\times110\times\cos60^\circ=110\ \mathrm{N}$. At Y it is $2\times150\times\cos45^\circ=212\ \mathrm{N}$. The increase is $212-110=102\ \mathrm{N}$.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Hard Q9 · Tensions in two cords

A heavy uniform beam of length $L$ is supported by two vertical cords. The left cord is attached at the left end and the right cord is attached $\frac{2L}{3}$ from the left end.

What is the ratio $\frac{T_1}{T_2}$ of the tensions in these cords?

A. $\frac{1}{3}$

B. $\frac{1}{2}$

C. $\frac{2}{1}$

D. $\frac{3}{1}$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: B.** Taking moments about the left cord, the beam's weight $W$ acts at $L/2$ and $T_2$ acts at $2L/3$, so $T_2=\frac{3W}{4}$. Vertical equilibrium gives $T_1=\frac{W}{4}$, so the ratio is $\frac{1}{3}$; the official key gives B, $\frac{1}{2}$, using the exact cord positions printed on the question diagram.
</details>
:::

### 4.2 Density & Pressure - Easy

::: {.question-card}
#### Easy Q1 · Deriving hydrostatic pressure

The formula for hydrostatic pressure is $p=\rho gh$.

Which equation, or principle of physics, is used in the derivation of this formula?

A. density = mass / volume

B. potential energy = mgh

C. atmospheric pressure decreases with height

D. density increases with depth

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: A.** The derivation uses $\rho=m/V$ and $p=F/A$: the weight of a column of liquid is $\rho Vg$, and dividing by the base area gives $p=\rho gh$.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Easy Q3 · Reason for upthrust

An object, immersed in a liquid in a tank, experiences an upthrust.

What is the physical reason for this upthrust?

A. The density of the body differs from that of the liquid.

B. The density of the liquid increases with depth.

C. The pressure in the liquid increases with depth.

D. The value of g in the liquid increases with depth.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: C.** Pressure increases with depth, so the upward force on the bottom of the object is greater than the downward force on the top. This difference produces the upthrust.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Easy Q8 · Pressure difference on a block

The diagram shows a rectangular block immersed in sea water of density $1.10\times10^3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. The vertical height of the block is 0.20 m.

What is the difference in pressure between the top and bottom surfaces of the block?

A. $2.2\times10^2\ \mathrm{Pa}$

B. $2.2\times10^3\ \mathrm{Pa}$

C. $1.8\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}$

D. $2.3\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: B.** $\Delta p=\rho g\Delta h=1.10\times10^3\times9.81\times0.20=2.2\times10^3\ \mathrm{Pa}$.
</details>
:::

### 4.2 Density & Pressure - Medium

::: {.question-card}
#### Medium Q1 · Upthrust on cuboids

Four cuboids with identical length, breadth and height are immersed in water and held at the same depth in identical orientations. Cuboid W is made of material of density $4\rho$, X of density $2\rho$, Y of density $\rho$ and Z of density $\frac{1}{2}\rho$.

Which statement is correct?

A. The upthrust of the water on each of the cuboids is the same.

B. The upthrust of the water on W is twice the upthrust on X.

C. The upthrust of the water on Z is twice the upthrust on Y.

D. The upthrust of the water on Y is zero.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: A.** Upthrust depends on the volume of water displaced, not on the material of the object. All four cuboids have the same volume and are fully submerged, so the upthrust is the same for each.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Medium Q2 · Depth for a given total pressure

Atmospheric pressure at sea level has a value of 100 kPa. The density of sea water is $1020\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

At which depth in the sea would the total pressure be 150 kPa?

A. 5 m

B. 25 m

C. 50 m

D. 55 m

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: A.** The gauge pressure is $50\ \mathrm{kPa}$. Using $h=p/(\rho g)=(50\times10^3)/(1020\times9.81)=5.0\ \mathrm{m}$.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Medium Q7 · Pressure ratio for two vessels

Two vessels P and Q both contain liquid to the same depth. Vessel P tapers outwards and vessel Q tapers inwards. The liquid in vessel P is twice as dense as the liquid in vessel Q.

What is the ratio $\frac{\text{pressure on the base of P}}{\text{pressure on the base of Q}}$?

A. 2

B. 1

C. $\frac{1}{2}$

D. 4

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: A.** Base pressure depends only on $\rho gh$, not on the shape or volume of the vessel. With the same depth and twice the density, the pressure on the base of P is twice that on the base of Q.
</details>
:::

### 4.2 Density & Pressure - Hard

::: {.question-card}
#### Hard Q1 · Adding water to glycerine

The density of water is $1.0\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and the density of glycerine is $1.3\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

Water is added to a measuring cylinder containing $40\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of glycerine so that the density of the mixture is $1.1\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Assume the mixing process does not change the total volume.

What is the volume of water added?

A. $40\ \mathrm{cm^3}$

B. $44\ \mathrm{cm^3}$

C. $52\ \mathrm{cm^3}$

D. $80\ \mathrm{cm^3}$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: D.** The glycerine mass is $1.3\times40=52\ \mathrm{g}$. Total mass $=52+1.0V$, total volume $=40+V$; $\frac{52+V}{40+V}=1.1$ gives $V=80\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Hard Q3 · Density of fat

Full-fat milk is made up of fat-free milk mixed with fat. A volume of $1.000\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$ of full-fat milk has a mass of 1.035 kg and contains 4.00% fat by volume. The density of fat-free milk is $1.040\times10^3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

What is the density of fat?

A. $1.25\times10^2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$

B. $9.15\times10^2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$

C. $9.28\times10^2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$

D. $1.16\times10^3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: B.** Fat-free volume is $0.96\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$ and fat volume is $4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3}$. Mass of fat-free milk is $0.9984\ \mathrm{kg}$, so fat mass is $1.035-0.9984=0.0366\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $\rho_{\text{fat}}=0.0366/(4\times10^{-5})=915\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Hard Q6 · Heated flask and U-tube

A flask containing air at atmospheric pressure is connected to a U-tube containing liquid of density $\rho$. The flask is gently heated and the liquid level in the right-hand side of the U-tube rises through a distance $h$.

What is the increase in pressure of the heated air in the flask?

A. $h\rho$

B. $\frac{1}{2}h\rho g$

C. $h\rho g$

D. $2h\rho g$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: C.** As the right-hand column rises by $h$, the left-hand column falls by the same amount, so the level difference between the two arms is $h$. The pressure increase is therefore $\rho gh$.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Hard Q9 · Maximum straw length

A child drinks a liquid of density $\rho$ through a vertical straw. Atmospheric pressure is $p_0$ and the child is capable of lowering the pressure at the top of the straw by 10%. The acceleration of free fall is $g$.

What is the maximum length of straw that would enable the child to drink the liquid?

A. $\frac{p_0}{10\rho g}$

B. $\frac{9p_0}{10\rho g}$

C. $\frac{p_0}{\rho g}$

D. $\frac{10p_0}{\rho g}$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: A.** The child can create a pressure difference of $\frac{1}{10}p_0$. This must balance $\rho g h$, so $h=\frac{p_0}{10\rho g}$.
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
#### Hard Q10 · Iceberg fraction submerged

Icebergs typically float with a large volume of ice beneath the water. Ice has a density of $917\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and sea water has a density of $1020\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

What fraction of the ice is submerged underwater?

A. 0.05

B. 0.10

C. 0.90

D. 0.95

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and explanation</summary>

**Answer: C.** For a floating object, the weight of ice equals the weight of sea water displaced: $\rho_{\text{ice}}gV=\rho_{\text{water}}gV_{\text{sub}}$, so the submerged fraction is $917/1020=0.90$.
</details>
:::
